main.text: [III, 138] [col. 367] Chapter 2.
On Paul's viper, and why the Pharisees are called a brood of vipers.

A certain man, after a shipwreck, is said to have escaped safely to Libya, and soon after, while sleeping on the shore, [col. 368] to have died from the bite of a viper. On him there is a not inelegant epigram of Statyllius Flaccus in the Anthology, book 3, ch. 22.

Λαίλαπα καὶ μανίην ὀλοῆς προφυγόντα θαλάσσης Ναυηγὸν, Λιβυκαῖς κείμενον ἐν ψαμάθοις, Οὐκ ἑκὰς ἠϊόνων, πυμάτῳ βεβαρημένον ὕπνῳ, Γυμνὸν, ἀπὸ στυγερῆς ὃς κάμε ναυφθορίης, Ἔκτανε λυγρὸς ἔχις. τί μάτην πρὸς κύματ᾽ ἐμόχθει, Τὴν ἐπὶ γῆς φεύγων μοῖραν ὀφειλομένην; [Lailapa kai maniēn oloēs prophygonta thalassēs / Nauēgon, Libykais keimenon en psamathois, / Ouk hekas ēïonōn, pymatō bebarēmenon hypnō, / Gymnon, apo stygerēs hos kame nauphthoriēs, / Ektane lygros echis. ti matēn pros kymat᾽ emochthei, / Tēn epi gēs pheugōn moiran opheilomenēn?]

A shipwrecked man who had escaped the whirlwind and the madness of the deadly sea, lying on the Libyan sands not far from the shore, weighed down by his last sleep, naked, still suffering from his grievous shipwreck, a baleful viper killed. Why did he toil in vain against the waves, vainly fleeing the fate owed him on land? Something similar happened to Paul. For when he had barely escaped from shipwreck onto an island near Libya, a viper at once attacked him, but with a very different outcome: this attack proved fatal not to Paul but to the viper. Luke begins the story thus, Actor. XXVIII, 3: When Paul had gathered up a great quantity of brushwood and laid it on the fire. Others render: when he had assembled, when he had collected, when he had swept together. And the Syriac has ܫܩܠ, he brought, a quantity of brushwood. This is followed by Erpenianus. The other Arabic version uses a long paraphrase, which nevertheless does not capture Paul's meaning: وبينما بولس يدور ويفتش ليجمع حطبا كثيرا [wa-baynamā Būlus yadūru wa-yufattishu li-yajmaʿa ḥaṭaban kathīran] And while Paul was going about and searching in order to gather much wood. Basil, in Homily 9 on the Hexaemeron, says it in one word: φρυγανιζομένῳ τῷ Παύλῳ [phryganizomenō tō Paulō]; in Hebrew this would be מקשש, as in Num. XV, 32., whose feminine is מקששת in 1 Reg. XVII, 10. But since Luke has συστρέψαντος τοῦ Παύλου φρυγάνων πλῆθος [systrepsantos tou Paulou phryganōn plēthos], we can understand nothing else than that Paul rolled the brushwood together (for that is the proper sense of συστρέφειν [systrephein]), either to gather it into a bundle, or to move what was already gathered to the fire, since he was not equal to carrying the load. So when he was throwing the brushwood thus bundled into the fire, a viper, creeping out because of the heat, fastened itself on his hand. Sarmenta [brushwood] are properly the superfluous wood of a rank-growing vine. But the Greek φρύγανα [phrygana], which Luke uses here, is more general. For φρύγανα [phrygana] are so called in Greek ἀπὸ τοῦ φρύγειν [apo tou phrygein], from burning: any dry twigs that easily catch fire, in one word cremia [kindling]. Further, [col. 369] [III, 139] it is well enough known that vipers and other serpents of that kind everywhere burst out of brushwood and twigs of this sort. Hence in Palladius's Lausiac History, chapter 20, Macarius, while digging a well, πλησίον θρύων καὶ φρυγάνων ἐκεῖ κειμένων, ὑπὸ ἀσπίδος ἐδήχθη [plēsion thryōn kai phryganōn ekei keimenōn, hypo aspidos edēchthē], was bitten by an asp near rushes and brushwood or twigs lying there. And Lucian in the Philopseudes relates that Midas, a vinedresser, lay ὑπὸ ἐχίδνης δηχθέντα [hypo echidnēs dēchthenta], bitten by a viper: Ἀναδοῦντι γὰρ αὐτῷ τὰ κλήματα, he says, καὶ ταῖς χάραξι περιπλέκοντι, προσέρπυσαν τὸ θυρίον δακεῖν τὸν μέγαν δάκτυλον [Anadounti gar autō ta klēmata ... kai tais charaxi periplekonti, proserpysan to thyrion dakein ton megan daktylon]; For while he was tying up the vine shoots and binding them around the stakes, the creature crept up from there and bit the big toe of his foot. Damir, in the chapter الاسود [al-aswad], that is On the black serpent: وقال للذي قال انه يموت حل حطبك فحله فاذا فيه حيه اسود [wa-qāla li-lladhī qāla innahu yamūtu ḥull ḥaṭabaka fa-ḥallahu fa-idhā fīhi ḥayya aswad] And (Jesus) told the man whom he had threatened with death to untie his wood (that is, his bundle of wood); when this was done, a black serpent was found in it. Thuanus, On his own life, book 3: When we were returning in the morning from the nearby church, and all hurried to the fire, which was not yet well lit, a serpent leapt out of a bundle of wood that was wet, either from the rain or from the underground cellar from which it had been brought; when it was laid out and examined for a long time, it had the appearance of an amphisbaena. Thus Paul's viper came out of the twigs; nor did it touch him while he was bundling them, because it was then torpid with cold. For it was winter. Hence Prudentius, in the place cited above:

Paul, while he was eager to gather brittle shoots and heap up the pile for the hearth, thrust his unwary hand into the stacks, where a sluggish viper lay torpid with frost, twining the coils of its body in the brushwood.

But when Paul had thrown the brushwood in which the viper lay hidden onto the fire, it, either revived by a moderate sensation of heat or provoked by excessive heat, attacked Paul. As in the Fables of Gabrias:

Ἔθαλπέ τις γεωργὸς ἐν κόλποις ὄφιν, Ὥρᾳ κρύους· ἐπεὶ δὲ θέρμης ᾔσθετο, Ἔπληξε τὸν θάλψαντα, κἄκτεινεν τάχος. [Ethalpe tis geōrgos en kolpois ophin, / Hōra kryous; epei de thermēs ēstheto, / Eplēxe ton thalpsanta, kaktеinen tachos.]
And in Phaedrus, Fable 75:
A certain man picked up a snake stiff with frost and warmed it in his bosom, compassionate against himself: for as soon as it was revived, it straightway killed the man.

Further, this viper fastened itself to Paul's hand, καθῆψε τῆς χειρὸς αὐτοῦ [kathēpse tēs cheiros autou], namely in order to bite with hostile tooth. The Vulgate translator, Erasmus, Castalio, Beza render it attacked his hand; the Ethiopic, it hung from his hand; the Syriac and both Arabic versions, it bit his hand. Some of the Fathers seem to have held this very opinion. [III, 140] For thus Tertullian in the Scorpiace, of Paul: He scorned the bite of the viper. And Ambrose in the Hexaemeron, book 6, chapter 6: A viper bit Paul. And Prudentius,

After it had warmed in the smoky kindling, and fiercely loosened its stiffened neck, now easy to bend, it carried to the hand, with darting head, the barbs of its teeth; and Paul shuddered, bearing it clinging and hanging by its bite from the wound in his finger.
And Arator, book 2 of the Apostolic History,
— — — — whose hand the viper, bearing the demon's weapons, meeting the rising flames, pierced with its ancient ferocity, and gave a wound of cold poison in the fire. — — —

Oecumenius likewise: Ἡ ἔχις, τῇ τοῦ Ἀποστόλου χειρὶ τοὺς ὀδόντας ἐμβαλοῦσα· [Hē echis, tē tou Apostolou cheiri tous odontas embalousa] The viper, having driven its teeth into the Apostle's hand. I, however, think that the same God who, sending his angel, shut the mouths of the lions lest they injure the Prophet with their bite, Dan. VI, 22., restrained the viper so that it did not fix its harmful teeth in the Apostle's hand. This these words of Luke seem plainly to teach: ἔπαθεν οὐδὲν κακὸν [epathen ouden kakon], he suffered no harm [col. 370]. For one who had been bitten by a viper would not be said to have been free of all harm. Nor indeed does καθάπτειν [kathaptein] mean to bite, so far as I know, nor to hang or to attack, but to fasten, like the simple ἅπτειν [haptein]. Xenophon in the Cynegeticus: Ἐκ τῶν τριμμῶν εἰς τὰ συμφέροντα καθάπτων τοὺς περιδρόμους ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν· [Ek tōn trimmōn eis ta sympheronta kathaptōn tous peridromous epi tēn gēn] Fastening the nets to the ground from the paths to suitable places. An anonymous poet on the armed Venus, Anthology, book 4, chapter 12,
Τίπτε μόθων ἄτλητος, Ἐνυαλίοιο λέλογχας, Κύπρι; τίς ὁ ψεύσας συγνὰ καθᾶψε μάταν. [Tipte mothōn atlētos, Enyalioio lelonchas, Kypri; tis ho pseusas sygna kathapse matan.]

Why, since you cannot endure battles, have you been allotted the arms of Mars, O Venus? What liar has vainly fastened these burdensome things on you? Likewise περικαθάπτειν [perikathaptein], to fasten around: as in Dioscorides, book 5, the chapter On quicksilver: Περικαθάπτουσιν ἄμβικα περιαλείψαντες πηλῷ [Perikathaptousin ambika perialeipsantes pēlō], They fasten around a cup smeared with clay. And the noun καθαπτὸς [kathaptos], fastened. So in an old proverb in Hesychius: Καθαπτὰ λύεις [Kathapta lyeis], or, as others have it, κάθαμμα [kathamma] (wrongly κάθαρμα [katharma] in Suidas), that is, You untie things fastened, or knots, things which to others are δύσλυτα [dysluta], insoluble. Accordingly, in Luke's words καθῆψε τῆς χειρὸς αὐτοῦ [kathēpse tēs cheiros autou], Stephanus supplies ἑαυτὴν [heautēn] and renders it fastened itself to his hand. So Basil put it, relating the same story in the ninth Homily on the Hexaemeron: Φρυγανιζομένῳ τῷ Παύλῳ ἐνάψας ὁ ἔχις [Phryganizomenō tō Paulō enapsas ho echis], supply ἑαυτὸν [heauton], when the viper had fastened itself on Paul as he gathered brushwood [III, 141]. Yet others render it hung, because ἀφάπτειν [aphaptein] and ἐξανάπτειν [exanaptein] mean to hang on or to suspend: and there follows at once ὡς δὲ εἶδον οἱ βάρβαροι κρεμάμενον τὸ θηρίον ἐκ τῆς χειρὸς αὐτοῦ [hōs de eidon hoi barbaroi kremamenon to thērion ek tēs cheiros autou], when the barbarians saw the beast hanging from his hand. Others again render it bit, as if they had read καθήψατο [kathēpsato]. For καθάπτεσθαί τινος [kathaptesthai tinos] in the passive voice means to bite someone, yet not with teeth but with jibes and taunts. And indeed Chrysostom on this passage reads καθήψατο [kathēpsato] for καθῆψε [kathēpse]. But he takes it otherwise, namely for the simple ἥψατο [hēpsato], that is, it attacked. For he has this in the following exposition: Εἶτα ἔχιδνα, ἐκ τῆς θέρμης ἐξελθοῦσα, τῆς χειρὸς αὐτοῦ ἅπτεται· καὶ ὅτι ἥψατο, δῆλον ποιεῖ τοῦτο ἐκ τῆς ἐπαγωγῆς. [Eita echidna, ek tēs thermēs exelthousa, tēs cheiros autou haptetai; kai hoti hēpsato, dēlon poiei touto ek tēs epagōgēs.] Then the viper, coming out from the heat, attacks his hand: and that it attacked he makes plain from what follows. So it must certainly be rendered. For ἅπτεσθαι ἀνθρώπου [haptesthai anthrōpou] is to attack a man, as Stephanus proves from Plato, Thucydides and Plutarch. Hence many render καθῆψε τῆς χειρὸς [kathēpse tēs cheiros] it attacked the hand, as if καθῆψε [kathēpse] or καθήψατο [kathēpsato] were the same as ἥψατο [hēpsato]. But there is no need to change anything, nor to attach unusual meanings to a common word, since it fits perfectly to say that the viper fastened itself to Paul's hand. For a serpent is said to bind what it embraces with its coils. So in the greatest poet two snakes
Seize Laocoön and bind him in huge coils. — —

And in Plutarch's book Whether land or sea animals, a dragon, somewhat angry with the Aetolian girl whom it loved, τῷ μὲν ἄλλῳ σπειρήματι τὰς χεῖρας αὐτῆς ἔδησε πρὸς τὸ σῶμα, τῷ δὲ ἀπολήγοντι τῆς οὐρᾶς ἐμαστίγου τὰς κνήμας [tō men allō speirēmati tas cheiras autēs edēse pros to sōma, tō de apolēgonti tēs ouras emastigou tas knēmas], bound her hands to her body with the rest of its coil, while it lashed her legs with the tip of its tail. So Nicander in the Theriaca, line 475, warns one to beware lest the cenchris
— — — σε καταφλέξῃ, καὶ ἀνάγχῃ Πάντοθι μαστίζων οὐρῇ δέμας, — — [se kataphlexē, kai ananchē Pantothi mastizōn ourē demas]

it burns you and constricts the body, striking with its tail on every side. And Leo of Byzantium in the Boeotica, cited by Plutarch in the book On Rivers, says of the boy Cythaeron: Ὁ δὲ ὄφις, τοῖς κόλποις περισφίγξας, αὐτὸν ἀνεῖλεν· [Ho de ophis, tois kolpois perisphingxas, auton aneilen;] The serpent, having bound him tight in its coils, killed him. And Cicero, on Roscius, in the first book On Divination: At night, by the light of a lamp set beside him, the nurse, aroused, noticed the boy sleeping, encircled in the embrace of a serpent. And in the second book: About Roscius himself it may indeed be false that a snake was coiled around him. To this belongs the passage in Aelian's History, book 6, chapter 21, where the dragon that fights the elephant, τῷ τραχήλῳ περιερπόσας, θείνων τῷ οὐραίῳ μέρει, καὶ σφίγγων θατέρῳ, ἀπάγχει τὸ θηρίον ἀήθει βρόχῳ, καὶ καινῷ [tō trachēlō perierposas, theinōn tō ouraiō merei, kai sphingōn naterō, apanchei to thērion aēthei brochō, kai kainō], having crept around its neck, beating it with the tail end, and [col. 371] constricting it with the other, strangles the beast with a new and unaccustomed noose. And in the description of the caduceus in Macrobius, Saturnalia, book 1, chapter 19: [III, 142] These dragons are bound together at the middle of their coils by the knot they call the knot of Hercules.

There follows the judgment of the barbarians on this incident: And when the barbarians saw the beast hanging from his hand, they said to one another, “No doubt this man is a murderer, whom, though saved from the sea, justice does not allow to live.” The barbarians, that is, the Melitans. For Paul was then on the island of Melite, and the Melitans were counted as barbarians because most of the inhabitants of that island were neither Greeks nor Romans, but Φοινίκων, ἢ Καρχηδονίων ἄποικοι [Phoinikōn, ē Karchēdoniōn apoikoi], colonists of the Phoenicians or of the Carthaginians, as we have proved elsewhere from Scylax, Diodorus and Stephanus. Accordingly, in the First Punic War the Roman consul Atilius, in a naval expedition against the Carthaginians, ranged over and laid waste Lipara and Melita, famous islands of Sicily, as Orosius relates in book 4, chapter 8. And in the Second Punic War, T. Sempronius crossed from Lilybaeum to the island of Melita, which was held by the Carthaginians. On his arrival Hamilcar, son of Gisgo, commander of the garrison, with a little under two thousand soldiers, and the town on the island were surrendered to him. So Livy, Decade 3, book 1. And we have shown that the name Melite itself is Punic. The Melitans, then, were part of the Barbarians, like the other Punic peoples in Africa, from whom the region itself was at length named Barbaria. These, then, when they saw κρεμάμενον τὸ θηρίον [kremamenon to thērion], the beast hanging, that is, the viper, from the hand of Paul, etc. For θηρίον [thērion] signifies not only a beast in general but also a serpent, or a venomous beast. Thus Sirach. XII, 17. Τίς ἐλεήσει ἐπαοιδὸν ὀφιόδηκτον, καὶ πάντας τοὺς προσάγοντας θηρίοις; [Tis eleēsei epaoidon ophiodēkton, kai pantas tous prosagontas thēriois?] Who will pity a charmer bitten by a serpent, or any of those who approach beasts? supply venomous, that is, vipers or serpents. Dioscorides, book 1, the chapter On the chaste-tree: Τὰ φύλλα ὑποθυμιώμενά τε καὶ ὑποστρωννύμενα θηρία διώκει· [Ta phylla hypothymiōmena te kai hypostrōnnymena thēria diōkei;] which Pliny renders thus in book 24, chapter 9: By fumigation too, or when strewn beneath, they (the leaves) drive away venomous creatures. Hence throughout the books of the physicians θηριόδηγμα [thēriodēgma] and θηριόδηκτος [thēriodēktos] are used of one who has been bitten by a serpent, and θηριακὰ φάρμακα [thēriaka pharmaka] of remedies that help against venomous creatures. Of the same kind is the fact that for Josephus, Antiquities, book 2, chapter 5, Ethiopia is a land θηριοτρόφος [thēriotrophos], because it nourishes many serpents. And in Galen the Marsi are θηριοτρόφοι [thēriotrophoi], because they feed on serpents. And in Dionysius of Halicarnassus the letter Σῖγμα [Sigma] is θηριώδης [thēriōdēs], because it imitates the hissing of serpents. So too the same word חיה is for the Hebrews any wild beast, and for the Arabs a serpent. And among the Chaldeans the words חיוא and חויא differ little: the former means beast in general, the latter serpent. Thus in Luke, then, τὸ θηρίον [to thērion] is a serpent, and indeed a viper; and when the barbarians saw it hanging from the hand of Paul, to which it had fastened itself, they concluded that he was a murderer, that is, guilty either of homicide or of some other grave crime. The species stands for the genus. By the same figure one of the Furies is called Τισιφόνη [Tisiphonē], ἀπὸ τοῦ τίειν τοὺς φόνους [apo tou tiein tous phonous]; for she was believed to be the avenger not of homicide alone but of other crimes too. [III, 143] And this was the barbarians' reason for passing so barbarous a judgment on a holy man: they saw him, scarcely escaped from one evil, presently fall into another, as though ἡ Δίκη [hē Dikē] would not allow him to live. Ἡ δίκη [Hē dikē], that is, Justice, a goddess; for so the ancients called her. Hesiod, in the Works, verse 254:

Ἡ δέ τε παρθένος ἐστὶ Δίκη, Διὸς ἐκγεγαυῖα, Κυδνή τ᾽, αἰδοίη τε Θεοῖς, οἳ Ὄλυμπον ἔχουσιν, Καί ῥ᾽ ὁπότ᾽ ἄν τίς μιν βλάπτῃ σκολιῶς ὀνοτάζων, Αὐτίκα παρ᾽ Διῒ πατρὶ καθεζομένη Κρονίωνι, Γηρύετ᾽ ἀνθρώπων ἄδικον νόον, etc. [Hē de te parthenos esti Dikē, Dios ekgegauia, Kydnē t', aidoiē te Theois, hoi Olympon echousin, Kai r' hopot' an tis min blaptē skoliōs onotazōn, Autika par' Dii patri kathezomenē Kroniōni, Gēryet' anthrōpōn adikon noon]

But there is a virgin, Dice, born of Jove, renowned and venerable to the gods who hold heaven. And whenever anyone harms her, assailing her with crooked insults, at once, seated beside her father Jove, son of Saturn, she tells of the unjust mind of men. Orpheus, Argonautica, verse 349.
— — — τούτου δ᾽ ἐπιμάρτυροί ἔστον [toutou d' epimartyroi eston] [col. 372] Ἰθύντειρα Δίκη, καὶ Ἐριννύες αἰνοδότειραι, [Ithynteira Dikē, kai Erinnyes ainodoteirai,]

Of this (oath) let the witnesses be Dice the directress, and the avenging Furies. In Euripides' Medea, Jason curses Medea thus, after she had defiled her hands with the slaughter of their common children, verse 1389.
Ἀλλ᾽ ὁ Ἐριννὺς ὀλέσειε τέκνων, Φονία τε Δίκη· — — [All' ho Erinnys oleseie teknōn, Phonia te Dikē]

But may the Erinys of the slain children destroy you, and Dice, avenger of slaughter. Aristotle, or whoever the author is, at the end of the book On the World, where he speaks of the supreme God: Τῷ δὲ ἀεὶ ξυνέπεται Δίκη τῶν ἀπολειπομένων τοῦ θείου νόμου τιμωρός· [Tō de aei xynepetai Dikē tōn apoleipomenōn tou theiou nomou timōros] Him Dice always follows, to be the avenger of those who have fallen away from the divine law. In the Hymn of Orpheus to the Horae, Dice is one of the daughters Θέμιδος καὶ Ζηνὸς ἄνακτος [Themidos kai Zēnos anaktos], of Themis and of Jove the king. Chrysippus, in Gellius, book 14, chapter 4, presents us with a vivid picture of her: Παρθένος δὲ εἶναι λέγεται, κατὰ σύμβολον τοῦ ἀδιάφθορος εἶναι, καὶ μηδαμῶς ἐνδιδόναι τοῖς κακούργοις· μηδὲ προσίεσθαι, μήτε τοὺς ἐπιεικεῖς λόγους, μήτε παραίτησιν, καὶ δέησιν, μήτε κολακείαν, μήτε ἄλλο μηδὲν τῶν τοιούτων. ὃς ἀκολούθως καὶ σκυθρωπὴ γράφεται, καὶ συνεστηκὸς ἔχουσα τὸ πρόσωπον, καὶ ἔντονον καὶ δεδορκὸς βλέπουσα, [Parthenos de einai legetai, kata symbolon tou adiaphthoros einai, kai mēdamōs endidonai tois kakourgois; mēde prosiesthai, mēte tous epieikeis logous, mēte paraitēsin, kai deēsin, mēte kolakeian, mēte allo mēden tōn toioutōn. hos akolouthōs kai skythrōpē graphetai, kai synestēkos echousa to prosōpon, kai entonon kai dedorkos blepousa] etc. She is called a virgin to signify that she is incorruptible and in no way yields to the wicked; that she admits from them no modest speech, no plea for pardon or petition, no flattery, nor anything at all of that kind. For this reason she is rightly painted as stern and with a frowning brow, with an intent and grim countenance, etc. In Plutarch, in the book On the Delays of Divine Vengeance, if there are any who have not yet fully paid the penalty of their crimes in this life, [III, 144] τούτους Δίκη μετὰ τὴν τελευτὴν ὁ δαίμων παραδίδωσι [toutous Dikē meta tēn teleutēn ho daimōn paradidōsi], these the daemon after death hands over to Dice to be punished more severely. In Aratus' Phaenomena we read that in the golden age she lived familiarly with men; in the silver age too, though more rarely; but in the bronze age, after they began to eat the working oxen, she withdrew to heaven,

— — — πρῶτοι δὲ βοῶν ἐπάσαντ᾽ ἀροτήρων, Καὶ τότε μισήσασα Δίκη κείνων γένος ἀνδρῶν Ἔπταθ’ ὑπουρανίη. — — — — [prōtoi de boōn epasant' arotērōn, Kai tote misēsasa Dikē keinōn genos andrōn Eptath' hypouraniē]
Alluding to which Nazianzen says in his third Poem,

Παρθενικὴ δ᾽, ἀπὸ σεῖο φυγὰς, πρὸς Χριστὸν ἀνέλθοι, ῞Ως τε Δίκη τοπάροιθε βοὸς κταμένου ἀροτῆρος· [Parthenikē d', apo seio phygas, pros Christon anelthoi, Hōs te Dikē toparoithe boos ktamenou arotēros]

Virginity, fleeing from you, will return to Christ, as Dice once did when the ploughing ox was slain. Nor is it surprising that the fame of a Greek goddess reached the Maltese, most of whom were Phoenicians. For before the Romans occupied Malta, rule over this island alternated between the Greeks and the Phoenicians, so that supreme power lay now with these, now with those, as we have proved elsewhere from reliable witnesses. It is to the worship of this goddess, then, borrowed from the Greeks, that they attribute the fact that Paul, snatched from the peril of the sea, at once fell into another, no less grave than the first. In this judgment one thing at least is pleasing: that they hold that the wicked by no means escape the penalty of the crime they have committed. For Plato says truly in the fifth book of the Laws: Τιμωρία δ᾽ ἀδικίας ἀκόλουθος πάσης· [Timōria d' adikias akolouthos pasēs] Punishment is the companion of all injustice. And Horace, book 3, Ode 2,
Rarely has Punishment, though lame of foot, abandoned the criminal who goes before her.

That vipers too are employed by God for the punishment of the impious is stated in Eccles. XXXIX, 35. (var. 38.): Θηρίων ὀδόντες, καὶ σκορπίοι, καὶ ἔχεις, καὶ ῥομφαῖα ἐκδικοῦσα εἰς ὄλεθρον ἀσεβεῖς [thēriōn odontes, kai skorpioi, kai echeis, kai rhomphaia ekdikousa eis olethron asebeis]; The teeth of wild beasts, and scorpions, and vipers, and the avenging sword, to the destruction of the impious. The Egyptians were convinced of the same about the asp called Thermuthis. Aelian, book 10, chapter 31: Φείδεσθαι μὲν αὐτὴν τῶν ἀγαθῶν, τοὺς δὲ ἀσεβοῦντας ἀποκτιννῦναι [pheidesthai men autēn tōn agathōn, tous de asebountas apoktinnynai]; that it spares the good, but brings death on the impious: and if this is so, says the author, τοῦ παντὸς ἂν ἡ δίκη τιμήσαιτο τὴν δὲ τὴν ἀσπίδα [tou pantos an hē dikē timēsaito tēn de tēn aspida], the justice of the universe would have honoured this asp: that is, the goddess Dike, who through it punishes the wicked, as is stated in what follows. Thus in the barbarians' judgement about Paul there was something not wholly to be despised. [col. 373] But it is also clear that in this same judgement they erred in many ways. First, in that they do not refer the punishment of the impious to the true God, but to an idol invented by men, which is called Δίκη [Dikē] by these, Themis by others, Astraea or Erigone by others, [III, 145] and by others finally Nemesis or Adrastia. 2. In that they act as though punishment were always exacted from the impious in this life, whereas it is often deferred to the life to come, where God compensates for the slowness of his judgements by their severity. 3. In that they think no one falls into grave calamity who is not also gravely guilty, whereas evils befall even the best, Job, for instance, and the man born blind, although neither he nor his parents were guilty of any notable sin, Ioh. IX, 3. Consequently no one's virtue or wickedness is to be measured by prosperity and adversity. Rather, judgement of hidden things must be left to God alone, who is the supreme arbiter of all. 4. They also err in passing a hasty judgement on Paul. For they do not wait for the outcome, but declare that he has already perished, as certain of his death as if it had already happened. Thus they speak in the past tense: Justice (or Dike) has not suffered him to live, like those who said of David, Ps. XLI, 9. Some grave crime clings to him, and he who has lain down will rise no more. Yet David rose from his bed, contrary to what they had supposed. And the same happened here to Paul. For he did not perish from the bite of the viper, which the barbarians saw hanging from his hand.

Indeed, when he had shaken off the beast into the fire, he suffered no harm. Thus was fulfilled what Christ had promised the Apostles, that they would take up serpents, Marc. XVI, 18. And that serpent seems to have fastened itself to Paul's hand not to harm it but to adorn it. For among the ancients there was, among the kinds of bracelets, the ὄφις ἐπικάρπιος [ophis epikarpios] or περιβραχιόνιος [peribrachionios], mentioned by Nicostratus in Athenaeus, by Philostratus, Epistle 39, by Hesychius and others; just as a necklace is described by Nonnus, Dionysiaca book 5, which
Ὡς ὄφις ἦν ἑλικῶδες ἔχων δέμας, [Hōs ophis ēn helikōdes echōn demas,]

Was like a serpent, having a twisted body. If we believe Oecumenius, the viper threw itself into the fire of its own accord, as if exacting punishment from itself for having attacked a body that in no way belonged to it: Κατὰ τῆς πυρᾶς ἥλατο, he says, ὥσπερ δίκας ἑαυτὴν εἰσπραττομένη, ὅτι τῷ μηδαμόθεν προσήκοντι προσέβαλε σώματι [Kata tēs pyras hēlato … hōsper dikas heautēn eisprattomenē, hoti tō mēdamothen prosēkonti prosebale sōmati]. But Luke expressly states that Paul shook it off, and into the nearby fire, not far off into the air, as we have it in Prudentius:
And he shakes off the asp, flung far away: the snake, cast off, beats the air.
This they refer to the old serpent, that is, the devil, who, having attacked the faithful in vain, was thrust down into the fire of Gehenna. Arator, in the place cited above:

— — — for the beast hanging from his finger is shaken off, flung onto the pyre, fitly given back to the flame, [III, 146] since it had first given that flame itself, which brought forth the fire of guilt, whence Gehenna burns. — — —

This was Paul's miracle, wholly unforeseen by the barbarians, who had supposed αὐτὸν μέλλειν πίμπρασθαι, ἢ καταπίπτειν ἄφνω νεκρὸν [auton mellein pimprasthai, ē katapiptein aphnō nekron], that he would swell up, or suddenly fall down dead. Πίμπρασθαι [Pimprasthai] properly means to burn and to be burnt up; then also to be puffed up by heat and to swell. Hesychius: Πιμπρᾷν· ἐμπυρίζειν, φυσᾶν, καίειν [Pimpran: empyrizein, physan, kaiein]. Aelian, book 1, chapter 57, says that the Psylli easily heal those bitten by the cerastes, provided they are called πρὶν ἢ πρηθῆναι τὸ πᾶν σῶμα [prin ē prēthēnai to pan sōma], that is, before the whole body swells. For Dioscorides writes that their whole body swells like varicose veins. The Etymologicum, on the buprestis, a kind of herb: Βούπρηστις δέ, φασι, λέγεται διὰ τὸ τοὺς γευσαμένους αὐτῆς μεγάλως πίμπρασθαι, τουτέστι φυσᾶσθαι [Bouprēstis de, phasi, legetai dia to tous geusamenous autēs megalōs pimprasthai, toutesti physasthai]; It is called buprestis, they say, because those who taste it swell up greatly, which in Greek is πίμπρασθαι [pimprasthai]. And Nicander on the buprestis, the animal, Alexipharmaca line 344:
Ἡ καί που δαμάλεις ἐριγάστορας ἄλλο τε μόσχους [Hē kai pou damaleis erigastoras allo te moschous] [col. 374] Πίμπραται, [Pimpratai,] — — — — —
Which sometimes swells heifers, sometimes pot-bellied calves. And in the Theriaca on the haemorrhous, line 306:
Τῆς γὰρ ὀδαξομένης τὰ μὲν ἀθροὰ πίμπραται οὖλα, [Tēs gar odaxomenēs ta men athroa pimpratai oula,]

When she bites, the whole gums swell, or else burn. For so the Scholiast: Πίμπραται· ὑποκαίεται, καὶ πυροῦται [Pimpratai; hypokaietai, kai pyroutai]. And a little later: Πυρακτοῦνται, καὶ ἀναβράζουσι [Pyraktountai, kai anabrazousi]. Nor is it taken otherwise in Lucian, when he says of the dipsas, πίμπρασθαι ποιεῖ [pimprasthai poiei]. For there follows: Καὶ βοῶσιν ὥσπερ οἱ ἐν πυρὶ κείμενοι [Kai boōsin hōsper hoi en pyri keimenoi]; And they (who have been bitten) cry out like those who lie in fire. In Luke, therefore, it can be rendered either way. Accordingly one of the Arabic versions has here: They expected that he would يحترق [yaḥtariq] burn. And Castalio: as they expected that he would burn. But Jerome: They supposed that he would be turned into a swelling, that is, that he would swell up. Arias and Beza follow this, and many other more recent writers. And not without reason, since among the symptoms that follow the bite of a viper this is one of the chief and most conspicuous: the bitten part swells at once. Dioscorides, book 6: Τοῖς δὲ ὑπὸ ἐχίδνης δηχθεῖσιν οἰδεῖ, καὶ ἐφ᾽ ἱκανὸν τὸ σῶμα ξηραίνεται [Tois de hypo echidnēs dēchtheisin oidei, kai eph᾽ hikanon to sōma xērainetai]; In those bitten by a viper the body swells and dries up severely. Nicander, where he treats of those bitten by a viper, Theriaca, line 240:

— — — φλύκταιναι ἀραιαὶ, Οἷα πυρικμήτοιο χροὸς, κλαδόωσιν ὕπερθεν· [phlyktainai araiai, Hoia pyrikmētoio chroos, kladoōsin hyperthen;] [III, 147] harmful swellings boil up on the surface, as if the body had been burnt with fire. So also Paul of Aegina: Pustules break out on the bitten part, as in burns. And Aëtius writes that from a wound inflicted by a viper there arises a bilious, hot, blistered, reddish swelling, etc. And Avicenna, in the chapter On the bite of vipers, at the foot of p. 137: ثم يظهر ورم حار احمر ذو بثور كثيرة ونفاطات كحرق النار [thumma yaẓhar waram ḥārr aḥmar dhū buthūr kathīra wa-nuffāṭāt ka-ḥarq al-nār] Then there appears a hot, red swelling, full of many blisters and pustules, as from burning by fire. These indeed agree. But against what is found at the end of the same chapter, واكثر ما يهلك يهلك في ثلثة ايام وربما بقي الي السابع [wa-akthar mā yahlik yahlik fī thalātha ayyām wa-rubbamā baqiya ilā al-sābiʿ] Most of those who perish, perish on the third day, and sometimes they survive until the seventh, it seems possible to object that the Maltese thought that Paul, bitten by the viper, would fall down dead on the spot, as though sudden death followed a viper's bite. I reply that according to Aëtius τοὺς ἐχιοδήκτους [tous echiodēktous] mostly die within seven hours. And in Pliny, book 11, chapter 53, the arrows of the Scythians, dipped in viper's gore, bring death at once by a light touch (though in the Mirabilia of Aristotle one reads only μιγνύουσι τῷ τῆς ἐχίδνης ἰχῶρι, καὶ οὕτω ποιοῦσι θανάσιμον [mignyousi tō tēs echidnēs ichōri, kai houtō poiousi thanasimon].). And in Pausanias' Boeotica a certain Phoenician relates ἄνθρωπον ἀποφεύγοντα ὁρμὴν ἔχεως, ἐπί τι ἀναδραμεῖν δένδρον, τὸν δὲ ἔχιν. ὡς ἦλθεν ὕστερος, ἀποπνεῦσαι πρὸς τὸ δένδρον τοῦ ἰοῦ, καὶ οὐ ζῆν ἔτι τὸν ἄνθρωπον [anthrōpon apopheugonta hormēn echeōs, epi ti anadramein dendron, ton de echin. hōs ēlthen hysteros, apopneusai pros to dendron tou iou, kai ou zēn eti ton anthrōpon], that a man, to escape the attack of a viper pursuing him, took refuge in swift flight up a certain tree; when the viper came there a little later, it breathed its poison upon the tree, and the man ceased to live. So among the Arabs جارية [jāriya] giaria is a kind of viper that kills at once. Hence Damir, in the Proverbs on the viper: رماه الله بافعي جارية وهي التي يموت لذيعها من ساعته [ramāhu Allāh bi-afʿā jāriya wa-hiya allatī yamūt ladhīʿuhā min sāʿatihi] God has cast him to a giaria viper, that is, has thrown him into an incurable evil: because whoever is bitten by this viper dies that very moment. For a viper's bite is more deadly according to its place [col. 375] or food, and if it bites when hungry, and in summer days, and when it has first been provoked. For then, with its bile inflamed, the poison becomes much sharper. Moreover, some bodies, and some parts within bodies, resist poison less. Since, then, there are so many causes why vipers kill by their bite either more slowly or more quickly, the time of the coming death cannot be fixed with certainty. But the viper that had attacked Paul could seem to have a most potent poison, because it had burst out of the midst of the fire more agitated and roused. So since a speedy death was feared from its bite, and the barbarians had waited a long time, and no harm had come to Paul, μεταβαλλόμενοι ἔλεγον Θεὸν αὐτὸν εἶναι [metaballomenoi elegon Theon auton einai], changing their minds they said he was a god, whom they had previously judged to be a murderer. Indeed, [III, 148] The rustic brood knows no measure.
And
While fools avoid vices, they run into the opposite ones.

As Paul was not a murderer, so neither was he a god, but a most faithful servant of God. Before, they sinned gravely against charity; now against faith. For, as Oecumenius notes, the gentiles were accustomed πάντα ποιοῦντά τι παράδοξον Θεὸν νομίζειν [panta poiounta ti paradoxon Theon nomizein], to take for a god anyone who performed something marvellous. Thus the people of Lystra decreed divine honours to this same Paul because he had healed a lame man; but a little later the same people stoned him: Act. XIV, 10. 19.

Many ask why the Jews, or the Pharisees, are repeatedly ^{a)} called γεννήματα ἐχιδνῶν [gennēmata echidnōn], brood of vipers. Most think that this alludes to the tradition that the viper is born by gnawing through its mother's womb, because the Jews showed themselves ungrateful toward God and the Prophets, whom they ought to have regarded as fathers. See, besides those who have written expressly on Matthew and Luke, Isidore of Pelusium, Epistle 105, and the Interpretations of the Parables of the Gospel ascribed to Athanasius, Question 20. To me it does not seem likely that a fabulous matter is alluded to, or that God and the Prophets are in this way compared with vipers. I therefore side with those who understand here the very wicked sons of very wicked parents. That is, κακοῦ κόρακος κακὸν ὠὸν [kakou korakos kakon ōon], A bad crow lays a bad egg. With this in view the martyr Stephen addresses the Jews thus, Act. VII, 51. O stiff-necked, and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit. As your fathers were, so are you also. And long before, David, Psalm. LXXVIII, 8: That they might not be like their fathers, a stubborn and rebellious generation, etc. Nor shall I much object if someone understands by the name of vipers the demons; why these are signified by serpents is known to everyone. Moreover, all who rebel against God are reckoned sons of the devil. Accordingly Paul calls the magician Elymas a son of the devil, Act. XIII, 8. And Christ says to the Jews, Ioh. VIII, 44. You are of your father, the devil, and you want to do the desires of your father. The δεινῆς ἐχίδνης θρέμμα [deinēs echidnēs thremma] in Sophocles' Trachiniae, line 1106, is something else. For there ἐχίδνη [echidnē] is not a viper but the fabulous Echidna, from whom Cerberus was born; for it is he who is spoken of there.

notes.text: Matth. III, 7. and XII, 34. and XXIII, 33. Luc. III, 7.
